title: Like a mother hen (Luke 13:18–35)
hookLine: how often I would have gathered you, as a hen gathers her chicks

cards: A warning arrives on the road. Some Pharisees come to Jesus, and it seems they're trying to help: "Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will kill thee."
Herod, the ruler of Galilee, the man who, Luke has told us, beheaded John the Baptist. This is a real threat.
Jesus sends back a message with a bite in it: "Go ye, and tell that fox" that I'm busy healing today and tomorrow, and on the third day I'll finish. A fox.
Hold onto that animal, because a few sentences later Jesus picks an animal for himself.

teach.b: He doesn't choose a lion, or an eagle.

He looks toward Jerusalem, the city he's heading for, and says, in the King James Bible: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!"

A hen, an ordinary farmyard bird. When danger comes, a hawk overhead, a fox at the fence, she can't fight it off. What she can do is spread her wings, call her chicks, and put her own body between them and harm.
So: Herod the fox, and Jesus the mother hen. One hunts. The other covers, even at a cost.
The image wasn't new. Israel's psalms had long pictured God's protection as wings.

teach.h: A HEN WITH HER WINGS OPEN.
teach.b: Psalm 91: "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust."
Jesus makes that old picture a mother's. And the lament is full of grief, not anger: how often I would have, and you would not.

teach.h: AS A HEN DOTH GATHER HER BROOD.
teach.b: The rest of the passage has the same open arms: people will come from east and west, north and south, and sit down in the kingdom of God; and some who are last will be first.

Then the week behind us: a sparrow not forgotten, a barn too big, a little flock, lamps burning, a tree given one more year, a bent woman standing straight, and now a hen with her wings open, over a city that might not come.

how: Some churches read Jesus' lament over Jerusalem in Lent, and on the Mount of Olives, the chapel of Dominus Flevit has a mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks.

s: in Luke 13, some Pharisees warn Jesus to escape from Herod
"get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will kill thee."
Jesus pictures himself as an eagle guarding Jerusalem
he chooses a hen gathering her brood under her wings.
the wings picture for God's protection first appears in this passage
the psalms used it long before: "under his wings shalt thou trust."

games.q: friends warn Jesus: Herod wants to kill you, leave now. what does he do?
o: he slips away to the desert.
he sends word to that fox: I'm healing today and tomorrow, and I'm going to Jerusalem.
games.why: "go ye, and tell that fox." he keeps healing, keeps walking toward Jerusalem, and then laments over it like a mother hen.

practice: Bring to mind the people you'd want under your wings, family, friends, the ones who've drifted, perhaps someone who has refused you.

Then picture them around your table with food and enough chairs, and notice who's missing, and who would be hard to invite. If you pray, hold each of them under those wings; if you don't, simply let each face stay a moment.

wordCard.voice: Hen. The animal Jesus picks for himself over Jerusalem, gathering her brood under her wings the way a mother covers her chicks from danger.

orig.note: Greek: a bird, and especially a hen. the word Jesus chooses for himself over Jerusalem.
